```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) format(round(x, d), nsmall = d)
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

Stomach contents are rarely identified to a single depth. A shrimp may be named
to species, a fish fragment only to "Pisces", and a bolus of digested tissue
to nothing at all. DietView keeps every one of those records, attaches a
taxonomic lineage to it, and lets you look at the diet at all ranks at once,
with the material that could not be identified below a given rank kept in view.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

This vignette runs one complete analysis on real data: the public extract of
the ICES Stomach Content Database that ships with the package as `ices_diet`
(ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the
R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`). It holds
`r big(nrow(ices_diet))` prey records from
`r big(length(unique(ices_diet$stomach_id)))` stomachs of
`r length(unique(ices_diet$predator_common))` predator species, sampled in the
North Sea, the Skagerrak-Kattegat and the Baltic Sea in 2020-2024. A small
invented table (`inst/extdata/dietview_example.csv`) is also installed, for
trying the mechanics on 24 rows. The vignette "A known diet" uses a simulated
survey, where the true diet is known, to show what keeping unidentified records
changes.

## 1. One row per prey record

```{r look}
head(ices_diet[ices_diet$predator_common == "Atlantic cod",
               c("stomach_id", "prey_name", "item_type", "digestion_label",
                 "prey_count", "prey_weight_g")])
table(ices_diet$item_type)
```

Each row is one prey record: a prey taxon found in one stomach, with its WoRMS
AphiaID, a count, a wet weight in grams and an ICES digestion code (0, 1 or 2).
The same taxon can appear in several records of one stomach, as `Aphia minuta`
does above, for example when prey were measured one by one. The readable labels
in `digestion_label` are inferred from the older ICES format, so check them
against the ICES vocabulary before you rely on them. There are no
taxonomy columns: DietView adds them in step 3.

Real data need a decision before any figure: what counts as prey? The
`r sum(ices_diet$item_type == "non_food")` non-food records (sand, stones,
plastic, wood) are not diet. Nematodes are mostly parasites of the fish, not
food, and there are many of them. We drop both, and say so when we report:

```{r filter}
# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]
```

```{r nem, include = FALSE}
nem <- phylum %in% "Nematoda"
nem_mack <- sum(nem & ices_diet$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel")
mack_before <- sum(ices_diet$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel")
mack_after  <- sum(dat$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel")
```

That removes `r big(sum(nem))` nematode records, `r big(nem_mack)` of them from
Atlantic mackerel, whose record count falls from `r big(mack_before)` to
`r big(mack_after)`. A choice like this changes the result more than any
setting in the package.

## 2. Say which column is which

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",   # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name      = "prey_name",       # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
dv_validate(dat, spec)
```

The specification changes nothing in your table. It records which column plays
which role, so the original data never have to be renamed, and it can be saved
next to your results. `dv_validate()` stops if a declared column is missing or
a weight is negative, warns about records with no prey key, weights that are
not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and ends with a one-line
description of the sample. Here it notes that
`r big(sum(is.na(dat$prey_weight_g)))` records have no weight; they count in
the record shares but add nothing to the weight shares.

## 3. Attach the taxonomy

The package ships a frozen WoRMS lineage for every AphiaID in the data: one row
per AphiaID, one column per rank.

```{r lineage}
ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in%
               c("Crangon crangon", "Gobiidae", "Crustacea", "Pisces"),
             c("prey_aphia_id", "scientific_name", "worms_rank",
               "phylum", "class", "order", "family", "species")]
```

Look at how incomplete identifications are stored. `Gobiidae` stops at family.
`Crustacea` (a subphylum) and `Pisces` (a superclass) have a phylum and
nothing below it, because they are coarser than a class. Those empty cells are
not errors. They record where identification stopped, and DietView keeps them.
The "Unidentified material" records have no AphiaID at all, so they get no
lineage.

```{r prepare}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
prep
```

With your own data you would normally query the World Register of Marine
Species once, read the matching report, and save the result as a lineage table
for every later run (the vignette on WoRMS shows how):

```{r worms, eval = FALSE}
prep_online <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")   # needs 'worrms' and an internet connection
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_online)                            # doubtful and unresolved matches
```

Saving the lineage fixes the taxonomic snapshot your figures were made from.
Note the date and the `worrms` version alongside it, because WoRMS changes.

## 4. Count the diet at every rank

```{r tree}
tree <- dv_tree(prep)
cls  <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")
head(cls, 8)
```

`value_occ` is the number of prey records assigned to each class, and `pct_occ`
its share of all records. `value_w` and `pct_w` do the same for weight. Every
record appears once in every ring of the tree: under the taxon it was
identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, in an `NA`
node below the last rank it reached. The denominator is therefore the same at
every rank, here all `r big(nrow(prep$data))` records or
`r big(round(sum(prep$data$prey_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)))` g, and each ring adds
up to 100%.

There are several `NA` rows because each sits under a different parent. The
tree says which:

```{r na-parents}
na_cls <- tree[tree$rank == "Class" & tree$label == "NA", c("parent", "value_occ", "pct_occ")]
head(na_cls[order(-na_cls$value_occ), ], 3)
```

```{r cls-values, include = FALSE}
g <- function(lab, col) cls[[col]][cls$label == lab]
na_par <- function(p) na_cls$value_occ[na_cls$parent == p]
```

The largest, `r big(na_par("NA|NA"))` records, is the unidentified material,
with no kingdom at all. The next two are records named only to a phylum or
something like it: `r big(na_par("Animalia|Chordata"))` fish recorded as
"Pisces", "Gnathostomata" or another name above class, and
`r big(na_par("Animalia|Arthropoda"))` arthropods recorded as "Crustacea" or
"Arthropoda".

The two currencies tell different stories. Malacostraca (shrimps, crabs,
amphipods and their kin) make up `r pct(g("Malacostraca", "pct_occ"))`% of the
records but `r pct(g("Malacostraca", "pct_w"))`% of the weight; bony fish
(Teleostei) make up `r pct(g("Teleostei", "pct_occ"))`% of the records and
`r pct(g("Teleostei", "pct_w"))`% of the weight. Records tell you how often a
kind of prey turns up; weight tells you how much it contributes. Report both,
or say which one you chose.

A note on names: `pct_occ` is a share of records. It is not the frequency of
occurrence (%FO) of the diet literature, which is the proportion of stomachs
containing a prey and does not add up across prey. `dv_fo_table()` gives %FO.
Take cod alone, prepared the same way:

```{r fo}
cod <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
cls_cod <- dv_rank_table(dv_tree(prep_cod), "Class")
fo_cod  <- dv_fo_table(prep_cod, rank = "class")
head(fo_cod, 4)
```

```{r fo-values, include = FALSE}
rec <- function(lab) cls_cod$pct_occ[cls_cod$label == lab]
fo  <- function(lab) fo_cod$pct_fo[fo_cod$taxon == lab]
```

Malacostraca are `r pct(rec("Malacostraca"))`% of cod's prey records but turn
up in `r pct(fo("Malacostraca"))`% of its `r big(fo_cod$n_total[1])` stomachs;
fish are `r pct(rec("Teleostei"))`% of the records and are found in
`r pct(fo("Teleostei"))`% of the stomachs. The two measures answer different
questions ("what share of the records?" and "how many fish ate it?"), and the
gap between them grows when a stomach holds several records of the same prey.

## 5. How much was identified?

```{r na-share}
na_share <- sapply(prep$ranks, function(r) {
  tb <- dv_rank_table(tree, tools::toTitleCase(r))
  round(sum(tb$pct_occ[tb$label == "NA"]), 1)
})
na_share
```

`r pct(na_share[["kingdom"]])`% of the records are unidentified even at
kingdom: that is the unidentified material. The share nearly doubles at class
(`r pct(na_share[["class"]])`%), where "Pisces" and "Crustacea" stop, and
reaches `r pct(na_share[["species"]])`% at species. A statement about species
would rest on fewer than one record in five, and digestion does not remove prey
at random, so that fifth is not a random sample. This is why DietView keeps the
unidentified nodes: they show how far a fine-rank statement can be trusted.

## 6. Draw it

```{r sunburst, eval = FALSE}
dv_sunburst(dv_tree(prep_cod), mode = "occurrence",
            title = "Atlantic cod, share of prey records")
```

The figure is interactive, so it is drawn on the package website rather than in
this installed vignette. The center is the kingdom ring and each ring outward is
one rank finer. White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that
rank. Hovering shows the count and the share. When you compare panels, build
one palette from the pooled data and pass it to every panel (see the article on
covariates).

## 7. Digestion

```{r digestion}
dg <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
sp <- dg[dg$finest_rank == "Species", c("digestion", "n_records", "p_records")]
sp$p_records <- round(sp$p_records, 1)
sp
```

```{r dg-values, include = FALSE}
sp_at <- function(lab) sp$p_records[sp$digestion == lab]
```

For each digestion stage, the diagnostic gives the share of records whose
deepest identified rank is species, genus, and so on, or none at all. The rows
above are the species share: `r pct(sp_at("0 pristine"))`% of the records at
stage 0, `r pct(sp_at("1 affected"))`% at stage 1 and
`r pct(sp_at("2 skeletal remains"))`% at stage 2. The digestion vignette reads
the whole table, predator by predator.

## 8. Before you report

- Say what you removed before the analysis (here non-food items and
  nematodes) and why.
- State the currency of every percentage: records, numbers or weight.
- Report the unidentified share at the rank you discuss (step 5).
- Give the taxonomic source and its date, or archive the lineage table.
- If you aggregated rare prey (`dv_aggregate_threshold()`), give the threshold.
- Archive the specification and the code with the figures.
- Acknowledge the data source: here "ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES,
  Copenhagen".
- Cite the package and the version you used. `citation("DietView")` gives the
  reference, "DietView: An R package for interactive, hierarchical
  visualization of predator stomach-content data".

## 9. Share it

```{r share, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet.html"),
              strata = c("region", "quarter"), length_col = "length_cm")
run_dietview(prep)   # interactive exploration, needs 'shiny'
```

The HTML file opens in any browser and needs neither R nor an internet
connection. It is a snapshot: it shows the data as they were when you built it.
The dashboard vignette builds one for the main predators, with length classes.
